Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child

Kocher criteria count · ultrasound for an effusion · aspirate at 3 or more · transient synovitis vs Perthes by the courseHow many Kocher criteria are present: aspirate now, or treat with NSAIDs and recheck?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • A febrile child who refuses to bear weight on a painful hip may have septic arthritis: count the Kocher criteria; 3 or 4, or an effusion with raised blood tests, means aspirate before antibiotics
  • Count the Kocher criteria: fever, non-weight-bearing, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) over 40 mm/h, white blood cell count (WBC) over 12,000/mm³. 3 or 4: aspirate; 0 or 1 in a well child after a cold: transient synovitis (toxic synovitis), rest and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)
  • Joint fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant, is septic: surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics
What it is

Septic arthritis: a bacterial infection of one joint, in a child usually blood-borne and usually the knee, hip or ankle

Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis): a sterile, self-limited effusion after a viral illness, the commonest nontraumatic cause of a limp

Bug

Staphylococcus aureus overall

Kingella kingae in children 3 years and under

Gonococcus in sexually active adolescents

Sickle cell disease: Haemophilus influenzae in the joint; Salmonella is its bone (osteomyelitis) organism

Spread

Blood-borne seeding of the joint in children

Age under 4, the commonest age (non-modifiable)

Sickle cell disease (non-modifiable)

An immunosuppressant such as methotrexate

Chain

Joint: bacteria seed the synovium pus fills the capsule the hip is held flexed, abducted and externally rotated

Damage: cartilage destroyed within hours or days femoral head blood supply lost osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) and growth arrest

Insights

The position shows an effusion, not infection. Transient synovitis can hold the hip the same way, so the count and the fluid decide PositionFlexion, abduction and external rotation lower the pressure inside the capsule, which eases the pain; an effusion of any cause does it.

Antibiotics before the tap hide the organism. Cultures are limited after prior antibiotics, so the blood culture and the aspirate come first

2Urgent risks
Septic hipFever, refuses to bear weight, pain on any motion of the hip

If 3 or 4 Kocher criteria, or a toxic child with an effusion, choose blood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration today, before antibiotics.

InfantMay be afebrile; ESR and CRP (C-reactive protein) may be barely raised even with pus in the joint

If an infant who will not move the leg has an effusion, choose aspirate; normal blood tests do not exclude infection.

ImmunosuppressedOne hot joint out of step with the rest, on methotrexate

If fever or septic fluid, choose treat as infection until the fluid says otherwise; no steroid into the joint.

3Differential
The painful hip in a child: most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis)Looks well, limps but walks; a cold days beforeAbout 5 days, up to 14; Kocher 0 or 1; normal radiograph
Septic arthritis of the hipToxic, febrile, will not bear weight; pain on any motionHours to days; Kocher 3 or 4; fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³
OsteomyelitisFever with point tenderness over the metaphysis; joint motion nearly fullAcute; bone, not joint: MRI, since radiographs typically lag over 2 weeks
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
Ages 5 to 10; gradual onset, afebrileLimp past 2 weeks; radiograph shows a flat, later fragmented femoral head
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
An adolescent who cannot rotate the hip inwardAfebrile; the hip radiograph shows the slip
Lyme arthritis
Usually the knee, less often the hipTick exposure in an endemic area; Lyme serology
Gonococcal arthritis
A sexually active adolescentFever, migratory joint pain, pustular rash
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Effusions in both hipsTransient synovitisScore Kocher; if 0 or 1, rest, NSAIDs and a recheck
Point tenderness over the metaphysis, motion nearly fullOsteomyelitisMRI
Sickle cell disease
H influenzae in the joint; Salmonella in boneTap first; the antibiotics must cover gram-negative organisms (a third-generation cephalosporin)
One hot joint on methotrexateInfection until the fluid says otherwise, not a flareAspirate; no steroid into the joint

Pause point. The bait: a recent cold read as proof of transient synovitis. A cold comes before both; the count and the fluid decide.

5Diagnostic criteria
Kocher criteria Fever – present · Non-weight-bearing – will not stand on the leg · ESR – above 40 mm/h · WBC – above 12,000/mm³ · CRP – over 2 mg/dL adds to the likelihood · Count – one point each; 3 or 4 aspirate; 2 aspirate if the child looks toxic or an effusion comes with raised blood tests; 0 or 1 observe · Confirm – joint fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or a positive culture By countBy criteria count in the 1999 derivation: 0 under 0.2%, 1 about 3%, 2 about 40%, 3 about 93%, 4 about 99.6%; fever was scored as over 38.5 °C. The rule has not been checked in other groups of children and may mislead when the risk is low.
6Severity
What sets the outcome
FindingMeansDo
Hours since onsetCartilage is destroyed within hours or daysDrain the same day; damage is preventable only if treated within 3 days
Infant or toddlerThe commonest age; blood tests may be normal despite pusTap an effusion even when the blood tests are normal (Urgent risks)
Bone tenderness or a slow responseOsteomyelitis alongsideMRI, as in Targeted tests
7Treatment
1

SynovitisKocher 0 or 1, well child

Rest and NSAIDs; ibuprofen shortened symptoms to about 2 days in a trial
2

Aspirate3 or 4, or an effusion with raised blood tests

Blood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration, before antibiotics
3

Septicfluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or pus

Surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics covering S aureus (vancomycin), the empiric target over 48 months
4

Raisevancomycin not working

Add a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) for gram-negative organisms
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
On NSAIDs: fever, refuses to bear weight, or no better in 24 to 48 hoursRepeat CBC, ESR and CRP; re-examine and rescore
Limp past 2 weeksRadiographs of both hips (Workup, Targeted tests)
Septic arthritis after drainageIV antibiotics until clearly improving, then high-dose oral for 2 to 4 weeks
Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy with 1 day of right hip pain refuses to bear weight on the right leg cries with any passive movement of the hip No trauma; no recent illness T 39.1 °C · WBC 15,000/mm³ · ESR 62 mm/h → Arthrocentesis → 4 of 4 Kocher criteria; draw a blood culture and aspirate before antibiotics
  2. 7-year-old boy with 2 days of left hip pain will not walk; lies with the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated screams with gentle passive rotation No point tenderness over the femur T 39.0 °C · WBC 14,000/mm³ · ESR 90 mm/h → Septic arthritis of the hip → Kocher 4 of 4; the position only shows an effusion (it occurs in transient synovitis too); motion this painful is the joint, not the bone
  3. 4-year-old boy limping since a cold 10 days ago today he refuses to bear weight on the left leg holds the left hip flexed and turned outward T 39.2 °C · ESR 78 mm/h · WBC pending → Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → fever, refusal to bear weight and an ESR over 40 are 3 of 4 with the WBC still pending; a recent cold does not make it benign
  4. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of a limp after a cold 10 days ago walks, favoring the right leg; well appearing T 37.9 °C · WBC 11,500/mm³ · ESR 18 mm/h · CRP 0.8 mg/dL (normal under 1) · ultrasound: effusions in both hips → Transient synovitis → Kocher 0 of 4; an effusion occurs in both diseases, but effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis (septic arthritis is usually one-sided): NSAIDs and a recheck
  5. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of right knee soreness and a limp began after gymnastics practice right knee: full, painless motion, no swelling or tenderness right hip: internal rotation limited and painful Afebrile · bears weight → Ultrasound of both hips → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip, which refers pain to the knee; ultrasound of both hips looks for effusions
  6. 6-year-old girl with 3 days of a left-sided limp well appearing; walks and bears weight mild pain at the end of hip rotation T 37.4 °C · WBC 8,900/mm³ · ESR 12 mm/h · CRP normal · ultrasound: small effusions in both hips → Arthrocentesis of both hips → Kocher 0 of 4: the needle is for 3 or more; treat and recheck
  7. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk ultrasound-guided hip aspiration: cloudy fluid 80,000 WBC/mm³, 90% neutrophils; Gram stain pending Blood culture drawn before the tap T 39.4 °C · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics → fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant: a septic hip is a surgical emergency, and antibiotics alone cannot decompress the joint
  8. 2-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of fever and refusal to bear weight on the left leg screams when the left hip is moved Ultrasound shows a left hip effusion; aspiration is planned T 39.4 °C · WBC 18,000/mm³ → Haemophilus influenzae → sickle cell disease (functional asplenia) adds encapsulated organisms such as H influenzae in the joint; Salmonella is its bone (osteomyelitis) organism; Kingella also fits his age, and gonococcus is the adolescent's
  9. 3-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk hip aspirate: purulent, 95,000 WBC/mm³, mostly neutrophils the operating room is not free until tomorrow Started on IV antibiotics after cultures T 39.2 °C · ESR 70 mm/h → Femoral head osteonecrosis → pus under pressure inside the capsule cuts off blood to the femoral head; delay also risks growth arrest
  10. 4-year-old boy with 4 days of a limp and left thigh pain point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis passive hip and knee motion nearly full and only mildly painful Well appearing T 38.6 °C · CRP 6 mg/dL · radiographs normal → Osteomyelitis → fever with point bone tenderness and preserved motion is bone, not joint: MRI; radiographs are normal early
  11. 5-year-old boy treated with ibuprofen for a post-viral limp 4 weeks later he still limps, worse after play hip abduction and internal rotation now limited No fever, night pain or weight loss T 37.0 °C · WBC and ESR normal → Radiographs of both hips → most transient synovitis resolves within 2 weeks; a limp past that needs hip radiographs for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  12. 11-year-old girl with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate wrists, knees and ankles improving 4 days of right shoulder pain, now waking her at night will not move the shoulder T 38.5 °C · synovial fluid 55,000 WBC/mm³, 80% neutrophils → Begin antibiotic therapy → one joint out of step with the rest, with fever and septic fluid on an immunosuppressant: infection, not a flare: antibiotics, then drain the joint; steroid into the joint or more methotrexate would feed it
  13. 4-year-old boy with 1 day of hip pain and a limp cold 10 days ago; no trauma appears well; no bony tenderness hip motion limited by pain Vital signs normal · ultrasound: small right hip effusion · CBC and ESR pending → Ibuprofen and a recheck → afebrile and walking, and he looks well, so treat and recheck; read the labs when they return (an effusion with raised blood tests then means aspiration); the ultrasound already answered the imaging question, and his pain needs treatment
Pairs with The Limping Child: an afebrile limp with no infected joint, sorted by age and time course. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent who cannot rotate the hip inward.
Transferable rule

A limp alone is not a reason to aspirate: score Kocher first.

Before ordering another test, name the question it answers that the last one did not.
